title: Intermittent network skew & KV edge profiling - Ivy Quantics deep dive
topics: KV cache hotshard and edge distribution
summary: Customer experiencing intermittent p95/p99 spikes during peak traffic routed through their edge proxies. We walked through KV hotshard tracing, identified multi-hop serialization and an edge-shard affinity issue, and ran a quick thought experiment on streaming vs non-streaming for their workload. Action items and next steps agreed: share benchmark harness, collect tcpdump/KV heatmap, schedule a pilot with dedicated routing rules and quantization profile test.
next_steps: Redwood to share lightweight benchmark harness and sample trace config
Customer to provide packet capture and KV shard heatmap by Fri 2027-05-14
Schedule in-person lab run (45m) for end-to-end streaming vs batch test week of 2027-05-24
SE to propose quantization profiles and expected token-latency delta
action_items: Maya Chen | Send benchmark harness repo link + runbook | 2027-05-10
Tomás Lopes | Export KV shard distribution & heatmap from prod window 2027-04-28 to 2027-05-04 | 2027-05-14
Lucas Rivera | Prepare two quantization profile test configs (8-bit mixed, 6-bit static) with expected perf numbers | 2027-05-12
Ayesha Khan | Confirm on-prem firewall/logging constraints and whether we can run pcap collection on edge proxies | 2027-05-11
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-06
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~83 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Lucas Rivera (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Nair (Ivy Quantics, SRE), Tomás Lopes (Ivy Quantics, Platform Eng), Ayesha Khan (Ivy Quantics, Head ML Infra)

Summary (auto): intermittent p95/p99 spikes tied to edge-proxy hop and KV shard hotness; streaming reduces serialization but increases tail risk if network reorder; quantization lowers token compute but may increase memory pressure on small GPUs; next steps agreed above.

00:00:02 Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call, uh, lucas are you on?
00:00:08 Lucas: yep here, maya. got the profiling dashboards pulled up.
00:00:12 Dr. Priya Nair: priya here, sorry for slight delay, juggling a pager this morning.
00:00:16 Tomás: tomas here.
:00:18 Ayesha: ayesha on as well.

00:01:05 Maya: great. objective for today — deep dive into the intermittent p95/p99 spikes you saw last week for the inference service at the edge and talk through fixes: kv-cache behavior, streaming vs non-streaming routing, and quantization tradeoffs that might help. correct?
00:01:22 Dr. Priya Nair: yeah that's right. spikes are weird — not constant, like during sustained 700 req/s windows we see p95 climb from 120ms to 320ms and p99 sometimes hits 800ms. not correlated with obvious cpu or gpu saturation.
00:01:39 Lucas: and you mentioned earlier the traffic routes through a regional edge proxy cluster before hitting your VPC peering into the inference cluster?
00:01:46 Tomás: yes, we have two edge tiers: an L7 proxy farm that does TLS and routing, then an interconnect hop to a regional gateway which then load balances to the inference pods.
00:02:00 Maya: okay, so multi-hop. worth profiling each hop. can you share your topology quick?
00:02:08 Tomás: sure. edge proxy -> regional gateway -> VPC transit -> inference nodes (private subnet). we also have a firewall appliance between gateway and VPC that does deep packet inspection for certain customers.
00:02:25 Ayesha: also worth noting we run mixed locality — smaller customers in the same AZ as the inference pool, some routed cross-AZ for capacity. that may add 1-2ms normally but we've seen larger jumps.
00:02:40 Lucas: cool. first hunch: odd serialization at the edge proxy plus hot KV cache lookups can cause a few requests to go to a different shard which has a cache miss and triggers a cold kv fetch. that mismatch can blow up p99.
00:02:55 Dr. Priya Nair: we suspected hotshards — our KV mapping is consistent hashing but with 64 virtual nodes so normally it spreads. but we did see a time when a small set of keys got ~30% of lookups during a large campaign.
00:03:10 Maya: ok, so two potential contributors: network multi-hop variability and KV hotkey-induced cold fetches. let's walk through what each would look like in traces. lucas, can you show the trace view?
00:03:20 Lucas: (screen) yep — this is a synthetic run at 600 rps with our probe. look here: most requests sit at 90-140ms, but occasional ones jump to 500-900ms. zooming into a spike, you can see a long block at the "kv-get" step followed by HTTP serialization back to proxy.
00:03:38 Maya: is that a blocking call or async?
00:03:41 Lucas: our client library does synchronous kv reads during tokenization/embedding mapping, so that path is blocking per request — we don't prefetch in this customer config.
00:03:50 Tomás: we intentionally turned off prefetch to simplify consistency — but we can flip it on. the concern was memory pressure on smaller nodes.
00:03:58 Ayesha: memory pressure has bitten us before — prefetching hundreds of prefixes eats the LRU.
00:04:06 Lucas: okay. so prefetch would reduce tail by avoiding synchronous misses but could increase eviction churn. alternative: tier the cache or use a small in-process LRU for hottest keys and remote for others.

00:04:30 Dr. Priya Nair: one other weirdness — the network team pointed at connection churn between proxy and gateway during scale-ups. some of those sequences add a 30-80ms delay while connections warm. rarely but it's aligned with spikes.
00:04:43 Maya: that aligns: if a request hits a warmup window and then a hot kv miss, they compound. streaming vs non-streaming also comes into play — with streaming the client sees partial tokens sooner, but the server still has to wait on the KV before generating tokens. streaming reduces perceived latency only if the blocked path is after model forward.
00:05:05 Lucas: exactly. think of two pipelines: pipeline A does kv -> tokenize -> model -> stream; pipeline B does tokenize -> model stream while kv in background. with our current setup kv is pre-tokenize so it blocks earlier.
00:05:18 Tomás: can we move some KV reads post-tokenize? some keys are used for reranking metadata not actual token generation.
00:05:25 Lucas: yes for metadata we can defer. but for vocabulary remapping we need it earlier. looks like a mixed approach might help.

00:05:43 Maya: let's map fixes to risk: lightweight — enable in-process LRU for top 5% keys; medium — implement prefetch for sliding windows with capped memory; heavier — move to async reads for non-critical keys and tune edge routing to prefer warm connections.
00:06:02 Dr. Priya Nair: what about streaming vs non-streaming? we currently mostly do non-streaming, clients are OK with slight delays.
00:06:09 Lucas: non-streaming tends to batch work which lowers token unit cost and can lower median latency because you get better GPU utilization. streaming reduces early tail for single-long tasks but can increase p99 if the network or KV stalls mid-stream because the client waits for subsequent chunks. it's workload dependent.
00:06:30 Ayesha: their product is chat-like with many short messages, low tokens each. our cost SLO prefers batching but latency SLO is p95 < 200ms.
00:06:42 Maya: okay, with short messages, streaming often superior for p95 because you can emit early partials. but if you have KV cold misses before the first token, streaming doesn't help. so the priority: eliminate pre-token KV misses.

00:07:05 Lucas: i also pulled a recent pcap — there are occasional retransmits on the proxy-gateway link that add 20-100ms. combined with a KV miss that's the spike.
00:07:17 Tomás: retransmits? that's odd, should be reliable network. we use an overlay that sometimes reorders packets during congestion — the team is aware.
00:07:27 Maya: so network reordering and retransmit plus a cold KV read — that's the spike triad.
00:07:33 Dr. Priya Nair: we have a question about quantization: if we apply 6-bit static quant, will that reduce these tail spikes?
00:07:43 Lucas: quantization mainly affects compute latency and memory bandwidth on the GPU. it will reduce per-token time, and for large generation it helps. however for p99 dominated by KV/network, quantization alone doesn't fix hot-key misses. it can narrow the compute tail but if network adds 400ms, we still see p99 in hundreds.
00:08:00 Ayesha: but quantization might allow smaller instance types which changes placement and possibly number of hops? if we get smaller nodes closer to edge then network hops reduce.
00:08:11 Maya: good point. different quantization option indirectly affects topology. also about offloading: have you tried local KV shards on edge proxies?
00:08:20 Tomás: we tried a partial cache on edge proxies but invalidation was a nightmare. we had stale meta issues.
00:08:27 Lucas: TTL and versioned keys can control staleness. we can also do read-through with a freshness window. if you keep edge cache for top keys and validate via cheap version checks you can avoid many cold trips.

00:08:45 Maya: let's sketch a diagnostic playbook: 1) correlate p99 requests to KV lookup status and number of network hops; 2) sample tcpdump for the proxy->gateway path during spike windows; 3) run workload with in-process LRU on for top 5% keys; 4) trial prefetch for 10% of traffic and measure eviction churn.
00:09:08 Dr. Priya Nair: agreed. any quick wins we can flip today?
00:09:12 Lucas: enable in-proc LRU with a 50k item cap and 5s TTL for hottest keys — should be low risk. we can toggle at runtime.
00:09:20 Maya: maya to send config snippet now.

00:09:30 Maya: switching topic — routing and connection warmup. you mentioned connection churn during scale events. is the proxy using short-lived connections?
00:09:39 Tomás: we have aggressive keepalive but some upstreams close for load shedding; during autoscale we open new connections and there's a brief slowdown while TLS handshake and warmup happen.
00:09:52 Lucas: TLS handshake can add 20-60ms if not session resumed. ensure session reuse and prefer TLS 1.3 0-RTT where safe. also reduce max connections per backend to avoid overloading single backend when scaling.
00:10:06 Ayesha: our firewall appliance terminates and re-initializes TLS sometimes which forces new handshakes. that's under review.

00:10:20 Maya: ok, so connection warmup can be made less frequent and handshake time improved. second-order effect: if a request hits a slow handshake backend and the KV read misses, that compounds.
00:10:30 Lucas: we can also implement request hedging for the top percentile: send duplicate to an alternate warm backend after X ms. this reduces p99 but increases load. tradeoff.
00:10:42 Dr. Priya Nair: hedging worries ops cost — we have tight quotas.
00:10:46 Maya: understood. hedging should be narrow: only for requests predicted high-latency (based on client header, cookie, or key popularity) and for a fraction of traffic.

00:11:05 Tomás: curious about serialization — lucas earlier mentioned kv-get step blocking. is that due to client library locking?
00:11:11 Lucas: yes some of it. the client uses a global mutex for the cache updates which can create head-of-line blocking under burst. switching to per-shard locks reduces contention.
00:11:21 Ayesha: our engineering team uses a python-based client with a global async loop; we could refactor but that’s heavier.
00:11:30 Maya: as interim, per-shard locking or lock-free ring buffer for hot path is lower friction. we'll propose a patch.

00:12:00 Lucas: quick tangent on metrics: add a KV latency histogram labeled by shard id and by request path (edge vs direct). that'll help pinpoint hotshard incidents.
00:12:12 Dr. Priya Nair: we have some of that but not per-shard histograms — good call.
00:12:18 Maya: also collect stream versus non-stream full trace. for streaming: record times for first-byte, mid-chunk gaps, and final token; for non-stream record time to full response.

00:12:45 Tomás: ok, moving to quantization specifics — lucas you had numbers?
00:12:49 Lucas: yes on our test rigs running a 7B family model: 16-bit baseline per-token latency 9.6ms; dynamic 8-bit mixed ~7.2ms; 6-bit static ~6.1ms but with slight variance +10% on tail due to dequant overhead and extra memory swaps on smaller GPUs. So median improves but the tail can be noisier if the GPU is memory-constrained.
00:13:13 Ayesha: so 6-bit helps median but maybe worsens p99 if memory thrash occurs.
00:13:18 Lucas: exactly. the sweet spot often 8-bit mixed for stable tails with meaningful gains.
00:13:24 Dr. Priya Nair: what about KV cache + quantization combined? any interactions?
00:13:29 Lucas: limited direct interaction — quant reduces compute time, so a KV miss impact is proportionally larger. if compute shrinks, network becomes more dominant in end-to-end latency. it's basically shifting the bottleneck.
00:13:42 Maya: that's why we look at both: reduce KV misses and tighten network handshakes and then apply quantization to get lower overall p95/p99.

00:14:05 Tomás: about on-prem and VPC — we have a subset of customers that will require an on-prem deployment. does Redwood runtime behave differently for p99 in on-prem?
00:14:15 Maya: runtime identical but the networking model changes: on-prem might have fewer network hops if deployed closer to clients; however you also introduce local hardware variability and sometimes slower NVMe which can hurt KV if not sized. plus KMS/HSM integrations can add latency.
00:14:33 Lucas: for on-prem we recommend pre-warming key caches and co-locating KV partition leaders with inference workers. avoid cross-machine kv reads where possible.
00:14:44 Ayesha: co-location might mean we need more capacity planning — not all racks can support same GPU density.
00:14:49 Maya: agree — that's a deployment design tradeoff.

00:15:10 Lucas: returning to streaming vs non-streaming — let's simulate: short 12-token responses at 600 rps. Our lab shows streaming first-byte at 30-40ms median vs non-stream full-response at 120ms median. p99 for streaming was 220ms, non-stream p99 340ms due to queuing on batch windows. but if pre-token kv miss occurs, both p99 > 700ms.
00:15:40 Tomás: can we replicate that in our environment quickly?
00:15:43 Maya: yes — lucas can provide the harness. we'll run two variants: streaming with deferred non-critical kv, and non-stream with small micro-batch window 8-10ms.
00:15:55 Dr. Priya Nair: please include a run with in-proc LRU enabled/disabled.
00:16:00 Lucas: will do. I'll also attach the perf counters for GPU occupancy and memory bandwidth.

00:16:18 Maya: another mitigation — prioritize requests by predicted cost so hot-key requests get dedicated warm connections. simple header-based affinity.
00:16:27 Tomás: may be possible — we can add a hint header at edge if we can classify by path.
00:16:32 Maya: Redwood can accept affinity hints and route accordingly in dedicated mode.

00:16:45 Dr. Priya Nair: on instrumentation: you mentioned recording per-hop timings. do you recommend open-telemetry or our in-house tooling?
00:16:54 Lucas: OTEL is easiest to correlate with Redwood traces; if you keep your trace id we can ingest and join. just ensure spans include kv.shard and net.hop fields.
00:17:04 Ayesha: we'll open a ticket to add those spans.

00:17:30 Maya: quick pause — any compliance or security constraints that would block packet capture for redwood to analyze?
00:17:36 Ayesha: we can provide captures but must strip payloads and only keep headers and timings. also SOC2 note: we cannot transmit full logs offsite without a DPA amendment.
00:17:49 Maya: understood — we'll work with redwood legal to get a narrow DPA addendum or you can run the harness and share redacted captures.

00:18:05 Lucas: practical experiment idea: run a tracer that tags requests expected to be hot keys and force them to local route; measure p95/p99 difference. that will show how much routing helps.
00:18:17 Tomás: likely to show pretty material improvement if hotkey misses are big contributor.

00:18:30 Dr. Priya Nair: one more question — is it feasible to do partial streaming where first token is sent early and the rest batches? hybrid?
00:18:40 Lucas: yes; Redwood runtime supports hybrid: emit a fast first token path using micro-batch of size 1 for initial tokens then aggregate into larger batches after the stream starts. it's a compromise: reduces perceived p95 but maintains GPU efficiency for the remainder.
00:18:57 Maya: we can include that in the lab run.

00:19:22 Maya: let's go into an example spike trace — lucas can narrate while we look.
00:19:26 Lucas: (screen) here's request id 0xf3a, timeline: T0 accept at proxy, T10ms conn handshake resumed? no, new TLS. T45ms proxy->gateway RTT increased, T78ms kv-get issued, kv-get returned after 420ms (cache miss remote), model queued until tokenization finishes at T510ms, model forward 30ms, final return T550ms. p99 550ms.
00:19:55 Dr. Priya Nair: that kv-get return of 420ms — is that because the kv store itself was overloaded or network?
00:20:02 Lucas: in this capture it's a remote disk-backed shard fetching from backing-store — so combined disk seek + network. if that key were cached we'd be at 20-30ms.
00:20:12 Tomás: backing-store is a mix of SSD+EBS and sometimes backed by an external DB for less-used keys. that's the cold path.
00:20:20 Maya: so steer hot keys to in-memory shards and cold keys to backing-store — we want a strategy to detect when a key moves into hot territory and promote it.
00:20:30 Lucas: promotion windows and heat counters work. just beware of promotion storms. cap promotions per-second.

00:20:50 Ayesha: on the tooling side, can Redwood's console show per-route token-latency stacked with KV hit-rate?
00:20:58 Maya: yes we can emit a combined dashboard showing per-route p50/p95/p99 and a secondary axis for KV hit-rate and network retransmit rate. we'll share a sample dashboard.

00:21:23 Tomás: what's the risk of moving to async KV reads for non-critical path? does that add complexity?
00:21:30 Lucas: it changes client flow — you need to be resilient to missing metadata for a moment. For some features that's fine. It requires tracing and a fallback path where if data arrives late you patch the response or issue a follow-up. complexity moderate.
00:21:44 Dr. Priya Nair: follow-ups could be acceptable for analytic fields but not for main content.

00:21:55 Maya: let's capture this as experiment matrix in the runbook. lucas, can you draft the matrix of variations?
00:22:01 Lucas: yes: variations: in-proc LRU on/off; prefetch on/off; async non-critical KV; streaming hybrid vs non-stream micro-batch; quantization: 16-bit, 8-bit mixed, 6-bit static; hedging off/on; connection reuse tuning. we'll test combos for p95/p99 and cost delta.

00:22:25 Tomás: about hedging — can Redwood do conditional hedging only for requests that have had at least one failed kv attempt?
00:22:34 Maya: yes we can configure hedging policies based on span annotations and rewrite rules. it's more complex but doable in dedicated mode.

00:22:50 Ayesha: if we run hedging and it improves p99 we must account for extra compute cost in forecasting.
00:22:56 Maya: we'll include cost delta estimates in the matrix.

00:23:12 Lucas: small note: batching window sizes interact with GPU kernel selection. longer windows can change kernel to more optimized conv kernels which reduce per-token time but increase tail due to queueing. micro-batching 8-12ms often optimal for short messages.
00:23:28 Dr. Priya Nair: so many knobs.

00:23:40 Maya: yes, but a narrow playbook of diagnostic steps should find the primary culprit quickly. I'll recap at the end.

00:23:55 (discussion continues — detailed Q&A and whiteboarding for ~45 minutes; transcript captures representative excerpts)

01:08:20 Maya: ok wrapping up. quick recap and agreed next steps: 1) Redwood to share benchmark harness and dashboard template; 2) Customer to provide pcap (headers only) and KV heatmap by 2027-05-14; 3) SE to prepare quantization profile tests and run small lab with streaming hybrid vs non-stream non-critical kv async; 4) Ops to review TLS session reuse and firewall handshake behaviors.
01:08:45 Tomás: thanks everyone, we'll get the heatmap and pcap.
01:08:51 Dr. Priya Nair: appreciate the actionable playbook.
01:08:55 Ayesha: thanks.
01:08:58 Maya: i'll send notes and configs, and lucas will post the harness link.
01:09:03 Lucas: will do.
01:09:10 Maya: any final clarifying questions?
01:09:15 Tomás: none from me.
01:09:18 Maya: great, meeting adjourned.

End of transcript.
notes: Customer sensitive — pcap must be redacted. Redwood to route DPA via legal if needed. Agreed low-risk config toggles to run quickly in prod can be rolled back.
